nodes.name: Lemma E.1: Invariance 1
nodes.statement:
Let $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ be a finite joint probability space, such that $|\mathcal{Z}| = q$ and $\alpha := \alpha(\mu) > 0$ is the minimum probability of any atom in $\mu$. Given parameters $k, d \in {\mathbb N}$ and $\delta > 0$, there exists $\tau = \tau((\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu), k, d, \delta)$ such that the following holds:
	
	Let $A : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ be degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials, such that, $\mathsf{Var}(A_j), \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(A_j), \mathrm{Inf}_\ell(B_j) \le \tau$ for all $\ell \in [n]$ and $j \in [k]$. Then, there exist degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials $\widetilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n \cdot (q-1)} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $\widetilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n \cdot (q-1)} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that, for all $i, j \in [k]$, it holds that,
	\begin{equation}
		\begin{vmatrix} \left \langle \mathcal{R}_i(\widetilde{A}), \mathcal{R}_j(\widetilde{B}) \right \rangle_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n (q-1)}} ~-~ \left \langle \mathcal{R}_i(A), \mathcal{R}_j(B) \right \rangle_{\mu^{\otimes n}} \end{vmatrix} \le \delta\;,
	\end{equation}
	where $\rho = \rho(\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{Z}; \mu)$ is the maximal correlation of $\mu$. In particular, one may take $\tau =  O\left ( \frac{\delta^{1.5} \cdot \alpha^{d/2}}{2^{O(d)} \cdot 2^{O(k)}} \right )$.
	
	Additionally, the theorem also works in reverse, namely, given degree-$d$ multilinear polynomials $\widetilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $\widetilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that $\mathsf{Var}(\widetilde{A}_j), \mathsf{Var}(\widetilde{B}_j) \le 1$ and  $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(\widetilde{A}_j), \mathrm{Inf}_\ell(\widetilde{B}_j) \le \tau$ for all $\ell \in [n]$ and $j \in [k]$, there exist $A : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that 36 holds.

nodes.name: Lemma D.3: Regularity
nodes.statement:
Let $(\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu)$ be a joint probability space. Let $k$, $d \in {\mathbb N}$ and $\tau > 0$ be any given constant parameters. There exists $h \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} h((\mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Z}, \mu), k, d, \tau)$ such that the following holds:
	
	For all degree-$d$ polynomials $P : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $Q : \mathcal{Z}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ such that, $\mathsf{Var}[P_{j}] \le 1$ and $\mathsf{Var}[Q_{j}] \le 1$ for all $j \in [k]$, there exists a subset of indices $H \subseteq [n]$ with $|H| \le h$ such that with probability at least $(1-\tau)$ over the assignment $(\xi_A, \xi_B) \sim \mu^{\otimes h}$, the following holds for any $j \in [k]$ (where we denote $T = [n] \setminus H$),
	\begin{itemize}
		\item the restriction $P_{j}^{\xi_A}(x_T)$ is such that for all $i \in T$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_i(P_{j}^{\xi_A}(x_T)) \le \tau$,
		\item the restriction $Q_{j}^{\xi_B}(y_T)$ is such that for all $i \in T$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_i(Q_{j}^{\xi_B}(y_T)) \le \tau$.
	\end{itemize}
	\noindent In particular, one may take $h = \frac{dk^2}{\tau} \cdot \left ( \frac{C_4(\alpha)}{\alpha} \log \frac{C_4(\alpha) \cdot k}{\alpha \cdot d \cdot \tau} \right )^{O(d)}$ which is a constant that depends on $k$, $d$, $\tau$ and $\alpha \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \alpha(\mu)$, which is the minimum non-zero probability in $\mu$.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.1: Multilinearize
nodes.statement:
Let $\rho \in [0,1]$, $\delta > 0$, $d, k \in {\mathbb Z}_{\ge 0}$ be any given constant parameters. There exists an explicit $t = t(k, d, \delta)$ such that the following holds:\\
	
	\noindent Let $A : {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B : {\mathbb R}^n \to {\mathbb R}^k$ be degree-$d$ polynomials, such that, for any $j \in [k]$ : $\mathsf{Var}(A_j), \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$. Then, there exist functions $A^{(1)} : {\mathbb R}^{nt} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B^{(1)} : {\mathbb R}^{nt} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ such that the following hold
	
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $A^{(1)}$ and $B^{(1)}$ are multilinear with degree $d$.
		\item For any $j \in [k]$, it holds that $\mathsf{Var}(A^{(1)}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(A_j) \le 1$ and $\mathsf{Var}(B^{(1)}_j) \le \mathsf{Var}(B_j) \le 1$.
		\item $\begin{Vmatrix} \mathcal{R}(A^{(1)}) - A^{(1)} \end{Vmatrix}_{2} ~\le~ \begin{Vmatrix} \mathcal{R}(A) - A \end{Vmatrix}_{2} + \delta$ and $\begin{Vmatrix} \mathcal{R}(B^{(1)}) - B^{(1)} \end{Vmatrix}_{2} ~\le~ \begin{Vmatrix} \mathcal{R}(B) - B \end{Vmatrix}_{2} + \delta$
		\item For any $\ell \in [nt]$ and $j \in [k]$, it holds that $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(A^{(1)}_j) \le \delta$ and $\mathrm{Inf}_\ell(B^{(1)}_j) \le \delta$.
		\item For every $i, j \in [k]$,
		\[ \begin{vmatrix} \left \langle A^{(1)}_i, B^{(1)}_j \right \rangle_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes nt}} - \left \langle A_i, B_j \right \rangle_{\mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n}} \end{vmatrix} ~\le~ \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{k}} \]
	\end{enumerate}
	
	\noindent In particular, one may take $t = O\left ( \frac{k^2 d^2}{\delta^2} \right )$.

nodes.name: Theorem 6.1: Gaussian NIS
nodes.statement:
Given parameters $k \ge 2$, $\rho \in [0,1]$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists an explicitly computable $n_0 = n_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ such that the following holds:

	\noindent For any $N$, and any $A : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$ and $B : {\mathbb R}^N \to \Delta_k$, there exist functions $\widetilde{A} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ and $\widetilde{B} : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to \Delta_k$ such that,
	\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}\left ( (A(\mathbf{X}),B(\mathbf{Y}))_{(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})\sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes N}},\ (\widetilde{A}({\bm a}), \widetilde{B}({\bm b}))_{({\bm a}, {\bm b}) \sim \mathcal{G}_\rho^{\otimes n_0}} \right ) \le \varepsilon\;.\]
	Moreover, there exists $d_0 = d_0(\rho, k, \varepsilon)$ for which there are degree-$d_0$ polynomials $A_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$ and $B_0 : {\mathbb R}^{n_0} \to {\mathbb R}^k$, such that, $\widetilde{A}({\bm a}) = \mathcal{R}\left ( A_0\left ( \frac{{\bm a}}{\|{\bm a}\|_2} \right ) \right )$ and $\widetilde{B}({\bm b}) = \mathcal{R}\left ( B_0\left ( \frac{{\bm b}}{\|{\bm b}\|_2} \right ) \right )$.\\
	In particular, one may take $n_0 = \exp \left ( \mathrm{poly}\left ( k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{1}{1-\rho} \right ) \right )$ and $d_0 = \mathrm{poly}\left ( k, \frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{1}{1-\rho} \right )$.\footnote{the details of the exact value of $n_0$ could be inferred from combining the bounds across various lemmas used. We skip it for brevity, and instead stress on the qualitative nature of the bound.}\\
	
	\noindent In fact, the transformation satisfies a stronger property that there exists an ``oblivious'' randomized transformation (with a shared random seed) to go from $A$ to $\widetilde{A}$ and from $B$ to $\widetilde{B}$, which works with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. Since the same transformation is applied on $A$ and $B$ simultaneously with the same random seed, if $A = B$, then the transformation gives $\widetilde{A}=\widetilde{B}$ as well.
